biography.name: Noah Sato

background.family: Lives with parents and a grandmother in an accessible rented house.
background.finances: Steady middle income; adapted recreation adds expense.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home; grandmother also speaks Japanese.
background.school: Public high school; uses a wheelchair because of a lifelong mobility disability.
background.accessOpportunities: Accessible transport and classes vary; family and school coordinate access.

timeline.story: In 2014, Noah staged races between toy animals and gave each elaborate rules. He used a small wheelchair and wanted cousins to stop moving his toys into spaces he could not comfortably reach.

At six, he joined an adapted recreation group. In 2017, he discovered that he liked competitive games but disliked adults cheering ordinary movements more loudly than they cheered an actual difficult shot he made.

In 2018, Noah became fascinated by thunderstorms and kept a notebook of weather observations. His grandmother helped measure rainfall, while he argued that a cloudy afternoon deserved more description than the worksheet allowed.

During 2020, online schooling reduced tiring building transitions and also removed casual conversations he enjoyed. Noah organized a weekly strategy-game call, learning that being the organizer did not mean getting to choose every game.

In 2022, an inaccessible field-trip bus initially excluded him from a science outing. After staff arranged another vehicle, he attended and loved the museum’s sound exhibit, while remaining irritated about the avoidable planning problem.

Across 2024 and 2025, Noah played wheelchair basketball and learned basic synthesizer software. He enjoyed both competitive teamwork and solitary sound experiments; neither interest replaced his habit of watching weather radar before outdoor plans.

At sixteen in 2026, he is comparing accessibility details at Texas campus open houses and asking about adapted intramurals. He wants to attend a music technology workshop, but transportation arrangements may determine which session is realistic. He recently invited teammates to hear an unfinished track and actually used their conflicting suggestions.

ambitions: Travel with friends
Combine electives across departments
He imagines independent city living with reliable access, friends nearby, and regular time for music and competition.
struggles: Occasionally skips events rather than negotiate access

biography.selfDescription: I am competitive about games and not especially competitive about grades. I like making strange sounds on my laptop, and I would rather people ask about that than treat every outing as an inspirational event.
openQuestions: Which campus access arrangements hold up in daily use?
Will audio interest deepen when he can use a studio?

biography.name: Samuel Price

background.family: Lives with foster parents and their adult daughter; placement has been stable since 2022.
background.finances: Current household meets needs reliably; Samuel has limited personal savings.
background.cultureLanguages: English; maintains selected family traditions from earlier homes.
background.school: Public high school; records from earlier school changes required reconstruction.
background.accessOpportunities: Caseworker, school liaison, recreation center, and foster-family transportation.

timeline.story: In 2014, Samuel enjoyed putting together floor puzzles with a relative and inventing names for the animals pictured. He liked explaining his choices but would quietly replace pieces when other children preferred a different arrangement.

At six, he started a school garden project and wanted to take seedlings home. During 2017, changes in family caregiving disrupted that plan, and he spent stretches in different households without a consistent outdoor space.

In 2018 and 2019, several school changes interrupted friendships and left gaps in topics taught in different sequences. Samuel kept a notebook of jokes, using familiar material to begin conversations when he entered another classroom.

During 2020, he lived with relatives and completed a mixture of remote and paper assignments. A teacher mailed drawing supplies, and he began sketching ordinary rooms from memory, including details other people had long forgotten.

In 2022, Samuel entered his present foster placement. Predictable meals and transport helped him settle, while a counselor gave him space to discuss changes without requiring every meeting to become a retelling of the past.

Across 2024 and 2025, he joined a recreation-center climbing group and started helping restore donated furniture. He liked learning specific techniques and surprised himself by enjoying a poetry unit after a teacher let students choose their examples.

At sixteen in 2026, Samuel is considering a Texas campus visit organized through school and a community woodworking course. He is interested but cautious about making promises, especially when program eligibility rules and transportation arrangements remain difficult to untangle.

motivations: Having possessions and plans that stay his
ambitions: Try a class that continues beyond one season
He imagines a stable home, lasting friendships, and enough independence to choose when to share his history.

biography.selfDescription: I usually want to know what happens after the first exciting day. I like learning a real technique, and I also like words that make an ordinary room feel different without pretending that everything in it is simple.
openQuestions: Which educational supports will continue after high school?
Does caution ease when plans prove dependable over time?

questions.scene: Someone has made several images about the same theme. They must decide which belong together, which need finishing, and how their order will affect what viewers understand.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine three pieces about change: a growing plant, a worn object, and a rearranged room. Consider a shared intention, a display order, and one piece you might leave out.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore developing a connected body of your own artwork and deciding how to present it? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Choosing a display order is only a small part of sustaining a personal body of work.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to develop a coherent personal body of artwork and make considered choices about how it is finished, presented, or adapted for an audience?

questions.scene: An old illustrated notebook has fragile pages and marks that help explain how it was used. Keeping it available for future study means preserving those details as well as its appearance.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine a torn page with faded writing and a stain from its original use. Consider which features future viewers might need preserved rather than cleaned away.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore preserving the original materials and meaningful features of objects for future study? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Valuing an old object does not establish interest in the careful material work of preserving it.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to preserve artworks, historical objects, or scientific specimens so their materials and significant features remain available for future study and display?

questions.scene: A delicate object is moving into storage. Future handlers will need a record of its condition, any work done, and instructions that protect it without unnecessary alterations.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine writing three headings for that record: current condition, changes made, and handling needs. Think of one detail that would belong under each for a fictional paper object.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore careful preservation records and storage or handling recommendations? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Making a short record does not show whether long-term documentation and prevention work would interest you.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to document conservation work carefully and recommend storage or handling conditions that reduce damage without unnecessarily altering the object?

biography.name: Cora McIntyre

background.family: Lives with parents and two brothers on a small acreage; grandmother visits often.
background.finances: Moderate income; one parent works remotely and one manages local accounts.
background.cultureLanguages: English; secular household with close ties to neighbors of differing beliefs.
background.school: Homeschooled through a cooperative with shared science and literature classes.
background.accessOpportunities: Flexible schedule, nearby community college, and limited large-group experience.

timeline.story: In 2014, Cora followed family goats around the yard and invented stories about their rivalries. She disliked formal worksheets but asked her parents to write down long explanations of what the animals had supposedly discussed.

At six, she began home lessons and a weekly cooperative class. During 2017, she enjoyed reading with older children, while group games confused her when other students changed rules they assumed everyone already knew.

In 2018, Cora took a community theater class and discovered that rehearsed conflict could be funny. She liked performing a strong-minded character but remained reluctant to speak when adults asked the real group to make decisions.

During 2020, her academic routine changed less than many friends’ routines did. She missed cooperative meetings and began exchanging hand-drawn puzzle letters with another student, making them increasingly difficult until neither could solve the last set.

At twelve, Cora tried a supervised livestock project and liked tracking feed and growth more than show preparation. In 2023, she also started reading essays that challenged opinions common in her family’s social circle.

Across 2024 and 2025, she joined a public-library discussion group and helped stage a children’s play. She found disagreement easier when participants had read the same text, but sometimes mistook a confident speaking style for a stronger argument.

At sixteen in 2026, Cora is exploring Texas dual-credit classes and a short residential literature program. She wants experience in a larger classroom and is unsure whether the freedom of home study has taught her enough about managing externally imposed deadlines.

ambitions: Try a class with unfamiliar expectations
She imagines adulthood with open land nearby, lively conversations, and freedom to revise her plans.

biography.selfDescription: I have had room to follow questions for a long time, which I appreciate. I also want to know how I do when the room is full of people who do not already know my family or how I learned something.
openQuestions: How will she adapt to a larger class and fixed timetable?
Which family assumptions will she retain after wider exposure?

questions.scene: A person gives a spoken or signed message to someone who uses another language. The message needs to cross languages accurately, without adding advice or leaving out an awkward detail.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine a fictional message: “I can attend Tuesday only if the time changes.” Restate it in simpler words without changing its condition; no second-language knowledge is needed.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore learning to convey spoken or signed messages accurately between languages? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Rephrasing in one language does not test language proficiency or the demands of interpreting in real time.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to convey someone’s spoken or signed message accurately from one language into another?

questions.scene: Someone says “That was interesting” with a doubtful tone. A word-for-word version in another language might sound enthusiastic, so context and intended tone need attention.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine that phrase said with delight and then with doubt. Consider what context you would ask about before choosing wording that preserves the intended message.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore working out meaning and tone across languages, including ambiguous messages? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Noticing tone here does not establish the language knowledge or sustained concentration the full activity requires.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to work out meaning and context across languages so the translated message preserves the speaker’s intent and tone?

biography.name: Theo Robinson

background.family: Lives with parents and a younger brother; relatives are nearby and generally supportive.
background.finances: Stable middle income with occasional budget limits for travel.
background.geography: Small town west of Temple, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English; active in a congregation where family maintains close friendships.
background.school: Public high school with modest electives; Theo is a transgender boy with supportive family and trusted staff.
background.accessOpportunities: School music resources, local theater, and family transport.

timeline.story: In 2014, Theo loved sorting costume pieces into possible characters and helping his brother build pretend shops. He could spend an afternoon inventing who owned each shop without wanting to act out the actual transactions.

At six, he began recorder lessons at school and liked matching sounds by ear. During 2017, he also became interested in weather instruments, making a rain gauge that collected more fallen leaves than useful measurements.

In 2018, Theo joined a children’s theater production and enjoyed painting scenery. He disliked being singled out for praise during assembly but happily explained his color choices to anyone who stopped beside the finished backdrop.

During 2020, he took online music lessons and helped neighbors organize contactless grocery deliveries. He liked solving small practical problems, while learning that being willing to help did not mean knowing every answer about unfamiliar requests.

At twelve, Theo began using his current name with family and later at school. In 2023, supportive adults helped establish ordinary routines, and he was relieved when conversations returned to music, homework, and disagreements about household chores.

Across 2024 and 2025, he played clarinet, volunteered with local theater, and grew curious about acoustics. A science teacher helped him compare how different surfaces changed recorded sound, and several early measurements proved too inconsistent to interpret.

At sixteen in 2026, Theo is exploring Texas music camps and a college science outreach day. He wants to meet people beyond his town while preserving the local friendships that make everyday life feel comfortable and familiar.

avoids: Being made a public example without asking
ambitions: Try a program beyond his home area
He imagines a home near trusted people with enough freedom to travel, make music, and choose his own routines.
struggles: Sometimes accepts too many small favors

biography.selfDescription: I want to be known well enough that people ask about the thing I am actually doing. I like sound and paint and useful little jobs, and I am still figuring out whether a bigger place would give me energy or just more noise.
openQuestions: Would a larger setting expand comfort or make routine access harder?
Does scientific interest deepen beyond the music connection?

biography.name: Caleb Hensley

background.family: Lives with mother and maternal grandfather; his father has been incarcerated since Caleb was twelve and they exchange letters.
background.finances: Grandfather’s pension and mother’s warehouse wages cover a modest rental; little money remains for extracurricular fees.
background.geography: Texarkana, Texas, after earlier years in eastern Kentucky.
background.cultureLanguages: White, English-speaking family with Appalachian roots; music and practical jokes remain important parts of family contact.
background.school: Public high school; attendance is consistent now after a difficult transition year.
background.accessOpportunities: School equipment, a youth music room, and nearby college or trade-program visits are available when work schedules allow.

timeline.story: Caleb liked sitting beside his father while he played guitar, copying the rhythm on an upside-down bucket. He also watched his mother sew curtains and repeatedly asked why one side of the cloth looked different.

He learned basic chords and sang loudly with cousins. His teacher described him as talkative during group work, but he also spent long stretches quietly arranging toy vehicles into elaborate parking lots with working entrances.

The family moved for work, and Caleb missed familiar relatives more than expected. A school custodian showed him where the music room was, and having one recognizable adult made the larger building less intimidating.

During remote lessons he helped his grandfather scan old photographs and identify people. He began asking questions about family stories that adults usually told as jokes, noticing how different versions left out different details.

His father’s incarceration changed household finances and made some classmates’ questions painful. Caleb argued more at school until a counselor helped him practice responses that protected privacy without requiring him to deny their relationship.

He started paid grocery shifts and borrowed a school guitar. Playing with two friends gave him a reliable weekly commitment; when one quit, Caleb learned to keep meeting without turning the absence into another personal rejection.

He balances school, work, and helping his grandfather with online forms. He wants education after graduation but worries about leaving his mother with more responsibilities; music remains important even when he cannot explain what place it should occupy later.

motivations: Contributing without losing his own future
ambitions: Wants postsecondary options to remain open
Imagines a dependable home with music and people who do not need him to explain everything.

biography.selfDescription: I don't want every fact about me to turn into a story about my dad. I like making things sound right together, and I'm still figuring out how school, work, and my family can fit together too.
openQuestions: Would he want to leave if household support increased?
Does formal music study appeal or would it change what he values about playing?

biography.name: Chinedu Okafor

background.family: Lives with parents and two sisters; family members support each other’s events while keeping different interests.
background.finances: Upper-middle income from pharmacy and information-systems work; family can fund several postsecondary options.
background.geography: Katy, Texas, near Houston’s cultural and educational institutions.
background.cultureLanguages: Nigerian American, born in Texas; English at home with Igbo conversation practice and frequent calls to relatives abroad.
background.school: Public high school with advanced science classes and an active dance program.
background.accessOpportunities: Private dance lessons, occasional observatory events, and campus visits are accessible with family transportation.

timeline.story: Chinedu copied his sisters’ dance routines and complained when anyone called his version cute. He also liked sorting picture cards into changing categories and explaining why a whale belonged with mammals rather than fish.

He joined a dance class where he was one of few boys and enjoyed the challenge of remembering sequences. His father attended every informal recital, including one where Chinedu forgot a section and simply waited for the music.

A borrowed telescope introduced him to the moon’s surface. He expected every night to reveal something spectacular and was disappointed until an astronomy volunteer showed him how repeated observation could make a familiar object more interesting.

During remote school he practiced dance in a cleared living room and kept a moon journal. His family negotiated noise and space rather than assuming that his activities should always take priority over everyone else’s calls.

He briefly entered science competitions, then chose fewer contests so he could remain in a dance ensemble. He liked laboratory work but found that prize preparation crowded out the questions he had originally wanted to investigate.

Helping younger dancers learn a difficult transition exposed his tendency to describe what movement felt like instead of what to do. He began trying several explanations and watching which one actually changed someone’s next attempt.

Chinedu takes physics, rehearses, and attends occasional night-sky events. He is considering education that could include both academic and artistic work, though he knows schedules may force choices; he wants to understand those choices before calling either interest secondary.

ambitions: Wants challenging education with continued dance
Imagines an active home life, late-night sky watching, and regular contact with extended family.

biography.selfDescription: People keep asking which interest is the serious one. They're both serious enough for me to keep showing up, and they're also both things I want to enjoy without winning something first.
openQuestions: Would formal artistic study appeal as much as ensemble participation?
Which constraints will matter most when science and rehearsals conflict?

questions.scene: A group of adult beginners is making short pieces of music, drawings, or performances. They want help developing their own expression and understanding why different creative choices have different effects.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Choose a fictional adult beginner who wants to express excitement. Imagine one question that helps them consider a creative choice instead of simply copying your preference.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore helping adult learners develop artistic expression and understand their creative decisions? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Enjoying your own creative activity does not establish interest in teaching adults to develop theirs.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to teach adult learners to develop artistic expression through visual art, drama, or music while understanding the choices behind creative work?

questions.scene: An adult learner shares a piece that does not match your personal taste. Useful feedback needs to consider their intention, explain what is working, and suggest a next step they can try.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine a piece intended to feel energetic but described by viewers as still. Form a feedback sentence about one observable choice and a possible experiment, without judging the person.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore evaluating creative work and giving constructive feedback that supports another person’s development? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Being kind about one piece does not establish interest in repeated, fair evaluation of students’ work.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to evaluate students' creative work or performances and provide constructive feedback that supports their development rather than merely expressing personal taste?

biography.name: Greta Halvorsen

background.family: Lives with parents and a younger sister; predictable routines leave substantial free time, and the family generally gets along.
background.finances: Comfortable income from corporate administration and physical therapy; parents have substantial college savings.
background.geography: Overland Park, Kansas, with an older cousin attending college in north Texas and relatives near Denton.
background.cultureLanguages: White, English-speaking family with Norwegian American grandparents; cultural traditions are mostly recipes and holiday gatherings.
background.school: Large public high school; ordinary college-preparatory classes and no fixed academic specialty.
background.accessOpportunities: Has many available activities and supportive adults, but has participated mainly where friends already go; Texas campus visits are easy to arrange.

timeline.story: Greta liked playing store with her sister and spent more time arranging shelves than deciding what to sell. She enjoyed visitors who followed her system and became upset when adults hurried the pretend checkout process.

She tried dance with a friend and liked the bus ride and matching costumes. When the friend stopped, Greta stopped too, without knowing whether the classes themselves had become boring or whether going alone felt too awkward.

A teacher asked her to help distribute classroom materials, and she noticed that labeled trays reduced arguments. She enjoyed the small improvement but did not consider it an interest because it looked less impressive than classmates’ hobbies.

During remote school she kept up academically and spent many afternoons rereading familiar novels. Her parents suggested several online enrichment programs; she attended one, felt little connection to strangers, and returned to chatting with existing friends.

She joined a service club because lunch meetings fit her schedule. Sorting winter donations was satisfying, while public outreach felt uncomfortable; she worried this meant she was not committed enough to the cause to belong.

Greta helped a neighbor organize a garage sale and discovered that answering straightforward questions from visitors was easier than persuading people to participate. She also tried hiking with cousins, liking short walks but declining a demanding overnight trip.

She now helps with service-club supplies and occasionally reads to children at the library. A cousin’s invitation makes Texas education options feel real, but she is still distinguishing enjoyment, familiarity, and willingness to persist when friends choose something different.

avoids: Assumptions that everyone has a passion
motivations: Becoming more independent in small steps
ambitions: Open to college in Kansas or Texas
Imagines a friendly neighborhood, predictable days, and enough time to read without feeling every hour needs a purpose.
struggles: Following friends instead of testing preferences

biography.selfDescription: I don't have a thing I introduce myself with, and sometimes that makes me feel behind. I like when a place works better because of something I did, even if nobody would call that an impressive hobby.
openQuestions: Which activities would persist without friends attending?
Does she prefer predictable work or simply need more supported introductions to unfamiliar tasks?

questions.scene: A community group has years of electronic forms, plans, and messages. People need to find the current version, know who may use it, and avoid keeping every file forever.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine five fictional files: an old plan, a current plan, a public notice, a private form, and a duplicate. Consider how each should be stored, found, shared, or eventually removed.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore organizing the full life of electronic documents and records? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Keeping your own files tidy does not establish interest in managing shared records across an organization.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to organize how an organization captures, stores, finds, shares, and eventually disposes of its electronic documents and records?

questions.scene: A shared record is useful to several teams but contains private information and must be kept for a set period. Access, retention, and eventual secure disposal need rules that fit together.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Using a fictional record only, imagine deciding who needs the full record, who needs a limited version, and what you must learn before setting a deletion date.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore balancing useful access, confidentiality, retention duties, and secure disposal? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: This example does not provide legal retention rules or establish readiness to handle confidential records.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to coordinate document-handling rules that balance useful access with confidentiality, retention duties, and secure disposal when records are no longer needed?

biography.name: Priya Menon

background.family: Lives with her father, stepmother, and an older stepbrother; sees her mother on agreed weekends.
background.finances: Stable finances; two households can both support activities but coordination takes effort.
background.geography: Plano, Texas; earlier childhood in Irving.
background.cultureLanguages: English is dominant; understands some Malayalam and uses a few familiar expressions with grandparents.
background.school: Public high school; swim team participant with uneven enthusiasm for academic competition.
background.accessOpportunities: Pool access, supervised safety courses, school resources, and reliable transport when schedules are coordinated.

timeline.story: Priya liked the apartment pool at four but refused to put her face in the water. Her father invented games with floating cups, and she gradually stopped needing him beside every step. At home she replayed animated films and assigned her stuffed animals parts, getting angry when adults changed their voices.

At six she joined lessons with a friend and discovered that she liked repetitive swimming better than the noisy games afterward. She was not the fastest child. Her instructor praised her willingness to try again, but Priya mostly remembers earning a snack and showing her mother the damp paper certificate.

At eight her parents separated. Switching bags between homes became a larger problem than either adult expected, especially when goggles were missing. Swimming remained enjoyable because the pool looked the same every week. She also spent cheerful weekends with cousins, whose elaborate outdoor games rarely involved any organized sport.

At ten she watched a lifeguard manage a minor poolside accident while another adult cleared space. The quiet directions interested her more than the injury. At a later supervised lesson she learned why people should call for trained help and avoid putting themselves in danger. She liked having an ordered first step.

At twelve she completed an introductory safety class using practice equipment and adult instruction. She remembered the sequence on a mannequin but spoke too softly in a paired drill. Her friend was louder and less accurate. Comparing them helped her notice that knowing steps and making yourself heard were separate problems.

At fourteen she swam on a school team and often timed practice laps for teammates. An online swimming group made every small setback sound disastrous, so she muted it during exams. When a teammate became dizzy, she summoned the coach and stayed nearby. The coach handled the situation; Priya felt shaky afterward.

Now sixteen she wants to complete the required training for a supervised pool job next summer if she meets the prerequisites. She likes swimming and concrete safety routines but does not enjoy being treated as the person who must always stay calm. She is practicing a firm speaking voice and still hates shouting across a room.

motivations: Knowing what first step is appropriate
ambitions: Complete eligible pool-job training next summer
Keep swimming after high school
supports: Friend who practices speaking with her

biography.selfDescription: I am calm-looking. Inside can be completely different. I like being told exactly what the practice situation is, but real life does not come with that part. I still want the training. Maybe I just want to be at the pool and get paid, which is also true. I do not have a big explanation for why swimming has stayed mine when I dropped so many other activities.

biography.name: Mateo Ruiz

background.family: Lives with his mother, younger brother, and mother’s partner; an older cousin is a frequent visitor.
background.finances: Household is financially tight following reduced work hours; basics are met with little spare cash.
background.geography: Laredo, Texas; relatives in Corpus Christi and Nuevo Laredo.
background.cultureLanguages: Spanish and English at home; comfortable switching in ordinary conversation, less confident with formal writing in either language.
background.school: Public high school; has made up missing work after a difficult transition to high school.
background.accessOpportunities: School Chromebook, public library, family receipt sorting, and a small neighborhood shop where he helps a known adult occasionally.

timeline.story: Mateo liked lining up toy buses and then making them crash into a pillow. His mother remembers the careful lines; he remembers the crashes. He spent evenings with cousins in the courtyard, inventing rules that changed when someone started losing. He liked being included and was rarely the one deciding the game.

At six he learned the walking route to a nearby shop beside his mother and memorized which houses had dogs. He liked carrying one small purchase home. School praise came mainly for finishing quietly, although he often copied the first instruction and missed the second when classmates were talking.

At eight he helped his mother put household receipts into envelopes. She checked all calculations. Mateo liked crossing a finished item off the list and once taped an empty envelope shut because it looked incomplete. An adult explained why looking tidy did not necessarily make a record accurate.

At ten he spent summer mornings with a shopkeeper his family knew. He arranged empty cartons and copied shelf labels, stopping when customers needed the aisle. He enjoyed the predictable opening routine. He disliked the afternoon crowd and preferred to go home for games with his brother once the shop became noisy.

At twelve a cousin showed him a budgeting app. Mateo entered fictional purchases for fun but lost interest when it required linking accounts, which he did not do. His school friend liked debating investing videos; Mateo was more interested in whether a price included delivery than in promises of quick gains.

At fourteen he missed assignments while trying to watch his brother and help with changing household schedules. He said school was pointless, although he was upset by failing marks. A teacher helped him build a short daily checklist. He improved through routine and reminders, without suddenly finding every subject interesting.

At sixteen he can reconcile a small list of purchases with receipts and flag missing entries for an adult. He enjoys setting up repeated work more than choosing new projects. Family members call him dependable, but he sometimes ignores messages when overwhelmed. He wants a steady adult life and cannot yet describe its contents.

activities: Checks household receipts with his mother
demonstratedSkills: Sets out materials in a familiar order
motivations: Having his own money without constant uncertainty
ambitions: Finish school on time
Have a steady adult routine; details unclear

biography.selfDescription: People say I am organized. My bag is not organized. I can organize a job if I know what the job is. Starting from nothing is harder. I do not have an inspiring answer about the future. A place to live, money for food, time to see people. I know that is not a whole plan. I wish people would let it be a beginning without laughing.

biography.name: Jalen Brooks

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger sister; nearby cousins visit most weekends.
background.finances: Stable working household with careful spending and one shared family computer.
background.geography: Garland, Texas; has lived in the same apartment complex since kindergarten.
background.cultureLanguages: Black American family; English at home; family gatherings often center on sports and food.
background.school: Large comprehensive public high school; generally attends, but completes little work in two classes.
background.accessOpportunities: School teams, neighborhood basketball courts, library, reliable phone internet, and parents who can occasionally provide rides.

timeline.story: Jalen spent preschool afternoons in his grandmother's apartment while his parents worked. He liked lining up toy cars by which ones looked fastest, then abandoned the arrangement when cousins arrived. Adults called him sociable because he followed older children everywhere. He was much quieter around unfamiliar adults and often let his cousin answer questions for him.

In first grade he learned to read on schedule but disliked reading aloud when classmates might laugh. Recess mattered more to him than classroom rewards. His father signed him up for basketball, and Jalen enjoyed the uniforms and postgame snacks as much as playing. At home he could spend a whole evening replaying one racing game.

By nine he knew which neighborhood children were good at which games and arranged teams so his friends stayed together. Teachers found him pleasant and easily distracted. He usually finished worksheets if someone sat nearby. He began asking for expensive sneakers after an older cousin explained which brands people noticed, although his parents rarely agreed to buy them.

During remote schooling he kept his camera off and sometimes played games after opening the required assignments. His mother discovered several missing projects late in the semester. The resulting restrictions produced arguments but did not create a lasting homework routine. Online matches became a reliable place to meet friends when visits and basketball practices were interrupted.

Returning to school, Jalen cared intensely about sitting with the right lunch group. He practiced basketball enough to make a school squad but disliked conditioning and eventually stopped trying out. A short relationship conducted mostly through messages ended awkwardly. He deleted photographs together but still checked the girl's posts. His grades varied according to how closely teachers monitored him.

He became the regular organizer of his friends' evening gaming sessions, remembering schedules and settling minor disagreements over team choices. In class, he could explain material verbally and still leave the written assignment blank. His parents argued about whether taking away his console would help. Jalen found their arguments embarrassing and avoided inviting friends over when tensions were high.

At sixteen he works one Saturday shift stocking drinks at an uncle's convenience store, a routine he finds tolerable when the store is quiet. He knows the shelves and notices missing products without prompting. He remains behind in English and chemistry. His closest friend has started making other plans, leaving Jalen unsure how much of their group will last.

motivations: Keeping his place in his friend group
ambitions: Wants a job that pays enough for his own car
Sometimes says he will keep playing competitive games; has no concrete plan
struggles: Attention divided between phone and homework
practicalConstraints: Parents cannot drive him to activities every evening

biography.selfDescription: I'm funny when I know people. Teachers say I could do better, which I already know, so hearing it again doesn't really help. I can remember everything about a game and forget one worksheet. I don't think that means I'm lazy at everything. Mostly I want people to stop asking what I'm going to be, because I don't have an answer that sounds good yet.

biography.name: Wyatt Mercer

background.family: Lives with his father and father’s partner; mother lives ninety minutes away, with visits that depend on transport and adults getting along.
background.finances: Household bills are usually paid but work hours fluctuate; two older vehicles require frequent attention.
background.geography: Rural community outside Abilene, Texas; school is a long bus ride away.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking white family; local connections through relatives, work, and hunting-season conversations, though Wyatt rarely hunts.
background.school: Small public high school; repeated absences and a long pattern of incomplete coursework.
background.accessOpportunities: Phone internet and some borrowed tools; few nearby programs, limited rides, and little active adult help navigating options.

timeline.story: Wyatt spent much of his early childhood at his aunt's house with several cousins. He liked cartoons, cereal, and sitting near the adults without being asked questions. He was not especially interested in the toy tractors people bought him because he lived in the country. His favorite activity was making the dog chase a battered tennis ball.

He learned letters more slowly than a cousin of the same age and disliked the comparison. By second grade he could read simple books but rarely chose them. His parents argued about money and household chores. Wyatt preferred sleeping at his aunt's because bedtime there happened at roughly the same time every night, although nobody called it a problem.

After his parents separated, school paperwork and weekend arrangements moved between houses unevenly. He forgot library books and sometimes missed the bus. A teacher let him finish work during lunch, which helped for a while. Outside school he mostly watched videos with cousins. He tried youth baseball for one season and was relieved when it ended.

His father moved farther from town, making visits to friends difficult. Wyatt became good at waiting: in vehicles, outside workplaces, and at the kitchen table while adults decided a plan. Remote schooling supplied very little structure. He logged in inconsistently and passed on a reduced set of work. The gaps remained noticeable when ordinary classes resumed.

He began missing school whenever he had stayed up late and could not face the bus ride. Sometimes he told his father his stomach hurt; sometimes he simply admitted he did not want to go. He liked a history teacher's stories but rarely completed the related assignments. Arguments about attendance became familiar and ended with threats that were inconsistently enforced.

Wyatt's father expected him to help clear scrap and hold parts during vehicle repairs. Wyatt could follow familiar instructions but was not fascinated by engines. He liked watching short comedy clips and playing one phone game. He briefly dated a girl from his bus route; the relationship mostly involved sitting together. Their breakup made the ride uncomfortable for several months.

At sixteen Wyatt is failing two courses and attending an afternoon credit-recovery period when he comes to school. He can work steadily stacking feed bags beside an adult he knows, but avoids asking strangers about openings. His father talks about him joining a relative's crew. Wyatt says maybe because he has not explored anything else and wants the discussion to end.

enjoys: Quiet time with his aunt’s dog
avoids: Long bus days after little sleep
Activities requiring meeting a new group alone

I know missing more makes it worse. Knowing that doesn't make me want to get on the bus tomorrow.

biography.name: Audrey Whitfield

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger brother; parents are attentive, busy, and highly involved in choices; conflict over dating and privacy remains unresolved.
background.finances: Affluent household with private tuition, travel, and paid enrichment available.
background.geography: Austin, Texas; family spends part of each summer with relatives in Colorado.
background.cultureLanguages: White American; English at home; nominal church affiliation, most social life through school families.
background.school: Small college-preparatory private high school; consistently good grades with substantial tutoring and scheduling support.
background.accessOpportunities: Extensive organized opportunities and reliable transport, but very little unsupervised exploration or paid work.

timeline.story: Audrey's days were arranged around preschool, swimming lessons, and appointments written on a kitchen calendar. She liked sticker books and telling adults what her younger brother was doing wrong. Her parents took many photographs and praised her willingness to smile. She enjoyed familiar visitors but became restless on museum trips chosen because adults thought they would be enriching.

She attended a small private elementary school where most children knew each other outside class. She learned how to follow classroom expectations and earned frequent good-behavior marks. Her mother tried piano lessons, tennis, and a children's art class. Audrey did not hate them, but she rarely asked to continue once the scheduled session ended or the equipment was put away.

A tutor helped her prepare spelling and math work twice a week. Audrey liked having someone explain exactly what would be assessed. She spent sleepovers making up rankings of favorite outfits and celebrities. A quieter classmate sometimes became the subject of the group's jokes. Audrey usually laughed along and has never considered herself the person who started them.

Remote school took place in a dedicated room with a reliable laptop. Her parents organized virtual activities when she complained of boredom. Audrey preferred chatting privately with friends while the official activity ran. She became very familiar with the appearance of other families' homes on camera and began noticing which possessions signaled that someone belonged in her social circle.

She returned to a school that talked frequently about leadership and future applications. Audrey joined clubs her friends joined and accepted a minor title that required almost no work. She received praise for a polished presentation after a tutor helped structure it. She knew the final result looked good but could not say which part she had actually enjoyed producing.

A relationship with a boy at another school occupied more thought than her classes. Her parents wanted access to her messages after she lied about where a group was meeting. Audrey viewed their response as humiliating; they viewed her refusal to explain as proof of poor judgment. The rules tightened, and she became more skilled at giving technically true, incomplete answers.

At sixteen she earns good grades, tracks deadlines carefully, and spends considerable time maintaining group chats and browsing resale clothes. She has no sustained hobby outside those social routines. Her parents discuss selective colleges as a shared family project. Audrey wants to go somewhere they cannot visit without planning, but has not separated that desire from interest in any course of study.

avoids: Activities none of her friends attend
activities: School social committees with limited duties
Weekend outings arranged with parental permission
ambitions: Wants to attend college away from home
Has no settled academic interest despite naming impressive options in adult conversations

My friends all sound like they have plans, but sometimes I think we're just saying what we said last time.

biography.name: Valentina Salazar

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger brother; grandmother lives in the same duplex; family sometimes disagrees about how much help to offer.
background.finances: Stable working-class household; discretionary spending is limited but essentials and school supports are covered.
background.geography: El Paso, Texas; extended family ties in Ciudad Juárez.
background.cultureLanguages: Mexican American; uses spoken English and Spanish, written messaging, and some ASL; bilateral hearing loss identified in early childhood, with hearing aids and school accommodations.
background.school: Public magnet high school; uses captioning and preferential seating; average-to-good grades.
background.accessOpportunities: School business course, accessible library programming, home phone and laptop; group activities vary in how well access needs are met.

timeline.story: Valentina liked covering the kitchen floor with pretend restaurant menus and assigning adults the same order repeatedly. Her family learned about her hearing loss after noticing missed responses in noisy rooms. Hearing aids and appointments became part of the household schedule. She still wanted the red cup, argued over bedtime, and preferred being read the same picture book every night.

In elementary school she learned to tell teachers when she could not follow an instruction. Adults sometimes praised this so enthusiastically that she wished they would move on. She liked drawing price tags and playing shop with a neighbor. At birthday parties she often understood the game after watching a round, although overlapping voices could make the jokes difficult to catch.

Her grandmother taught her simple sewing repairs, which Valentina tolerated because she wanted to alter doll clothes. The interest did not grow into a lasting sewing hobby. She preferred making short videos with cousins and adding exaggerated captions. At school she enjoyed straightforward arithmetic and became annoyed when classmates assumed a missed comment meant she did not understand the whole lesson.

Remote learning made some things easier because written instructions stayed on screen. Poor automatic captions created other problems. Valentina became quick at asking classmates to send the actual assignment wording. She spent considerable time in group chats discussing shows and classmates. Her parents thought she was studying more than she was because she almost always had the laptop open.

She entered a magnet program after her mother encouraged the application. Valentina liked the new building and initially regretted leaving neighborhood friends. She started browsing resale listings and noticed how photographs, descriptions, and response times affected which items sold. She sold a few outgrown clothes with parental supervision, enjoying the listing process more than arranging pickup with unfamiliar buyers.

A business applications class introduced her to inventory tables and simple cost comparisons. She liked organizing information for an actual small sale. Group discussions remained tiring when classmates spoke over one another, and she sometimes withdrew even after the teacher offered help. She had a brief relationship with a classmate who messaged constantly; she ended it because she wanted fewer demands on her time.

At sixteen Valentina manages a small monthly resale listing session with a cousin and keeps a simple record of costs and proceeds. She does not consider it a growing business yet. She likes clothes and social media but sometimes takes a week away from posting. Her family encourages a secure degree; she wants to compare ordinary work settings before agreeing that more school is the obvious next step.

Being treated as a lesson about perseverance

motivations: Being considered capable without excessive attention

biography.name: Cameron

background.family: Lives with parents and a nearby uncle who shares workshop time.
background.finances: Moderate income; technical study would require cost comparison.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family often exchanges practical help with neighbors.
background.school: Public high school with basic science and technical electives.
background.accessOpportunities: Bicycle work with an experienced relative and observation of engine maintenance.

timeline.story: In 2014, Cameron liked toy vehicles but also spent long afternoons making paper masks with cousins. Their favorite games involved something breaking in an imaginary journey and a character figuring out how everyone could continue.

At six, they learned basic bicycle care with an uncle. During 2017, they were impatient to replace a squeaky part, and the uncle showed how checking alignment first could avoid replacing something that was not actually broken.

In 2018, Cameron joined a recreation-center group and liked helping set up equipment. They enjoyed explaining a simple adjustment to another child more than selling raffle tickets, even when the sale supported an activity they liked.

During 2020, they used extra home time to clean a bicycle and keep notes with adult guidance. A repair that seemed successful failed its first check, making the final testing feel more important than the satisfying moment of reassembly.

At twelve, Cameron began logging bicycle repairs in a notebook. In 2023, they watched an experienced relative maintain an engine, asking what each check ruled out while leaving unfamiliar or potentially dangerous tasks to the adult.

Across 2024 and 2025, they continued supervised bicycle work and became curious about larger machines. Workshop routines and clear explanations to users sounded appealing, while prolonged desk research and sales conversations remained much less attractive.

At sixteen in 2026, Cameron is comparing Texas technical training in vehicle repair and industrial machinery. They want to see both settings before choosing, knowing informal repairs do not establish professional competence or reveal how daily workplace demands would feel.

ambitions: Compare vehicle and machinery training
They imagine a practical independent home with reliable transport, a small workspace, and time with friends.

biography.selfDescription: I want to know why something stopped working before I start changing parts. I enjoy the workshop, but I have only seen a small part of what repair work can involve, and I want to compare the real settings.

biography.name: Rowan

background.family: Lives with parents and an older sibling.
background.finances: Moderate income; occasional clothing purchases are planned.
background.cultureLanguages: English and Spanish within the family.
background.school: Public high school with art and career exploration events.
background.accessOpportunities: Style sketches and one supervised mannequin demonstration; no paid services.

timeline.story: In 2014, Rowan liked dressing paper figures and inventing where each was going that day. They also enjoyed large outdoor games, often changing clothes in the story more frequently than changing the actual game they played.

At six, they began drawing family members in imagined outfits. During 2017, a cousin pointed out that a favorite sketch did not resemble what the cousin wanted, teaching Rowan to ask before assuming a personal preference was universal.

In 2018, Rowan joined a school art group and enjoyed planning colors and shapes. Science experiments and keeping office-style lists held less interest, although they completed the required assignments and occasionally liked an unexpected topic.

During 2020, Rowan collected hairstyle references and sketched possibilities for fictional characters. They enjoyed listening when relatives described what felt comfortable, learning that a style could look appealing in a picture and still fail someone’s everyday routine.

At twelve, Rowan began asking more specific questions before sketching a style for someone. In 2023, a school exploration event introduced the idea of licensed salon training, which sounded worth investigating rather than like a settled decision.

Across 2024 and 2025, Rowan tried a careful technique on a mannequin under supervision and helped organize demonstration tools. They enjoyed the welcoming setting but had never provided a paid salon service or learned how demanding customer situations were handled.

At sixteen in 2026, Rowan is comparing Texas licensed training information and introductory visits. They like spending some money on clothing, but want a realistic view of customer work, practice requirements, and the difference between visual interest and a longer training commitment.

avoids: Science experiments as a main activity
ambitions: Explore licensed training and customer settings
They imagine a friendly adult routine with a comfortable home, personal style, and close social connections.
struggles: May assume a welcoming event reflects all workdays

biography.selfDescription: I like hearing what somebody actually wants before I start drawing an idea. The demonstration was interesting, but a mannequin does not ask difficult questions or have a long day, so I know I still have a lot to see.
openQuestions: How does interest change with repetitive technical practice?
Would sustained customer interaction feel energizing or tiring?

questions.scene: A design must be made by people who did not create the original idea. They need clear details about materials, fit, and construction, including how to handle practical limits without losing the intended look.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine someone else must make a fictional bag from your description. Name a measurement, a material detail, and an intended effect you would explain so they do not have to guess.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore communicating production details and balancing an intended look with practical making constraints? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Describing one object does not establish interest in sustained production communication and revisions.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to communicate clear production details and balance the intended look with fit, materials, and practical constraints so others can make the design?

questions.scene: Someone has made several images about the same theme. They must decide which belong together, which need finishing, and how their order will affect what viewers understand.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine three pieces about change: a growing plant, a worn object, and a rearranged room. Consider a shared intention, a display order, and one piece you might leave out.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore developing a connected body of your own artwork and deciding how to present it? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Choosing a display order is only a small part of sustaining a personal body of work.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to develop a coherent personal body of artwork and make considered choices about how it is finished, presented, or adapted for an audience?

biography.name: Jordan

background.family: Lives with parents and an older brother.
background.finances: Moderate income; practical training costs need comparison.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family takes part in local volunteer events.
background.school: Public high school with access to an introductory first-aid course.
background.accessOpportunities: Instructor-led scenarios only; no independent emergency care.

timeline.story: In 2014, Jordan liked relay games and inventing sequences everyone had to follow. She also drew colorful maps for imagined islands, usually leaving the destination undecided until the rest of the game was already underway.

At six, she began helping arrange supplies for community events. During 2017, she learned that being ready for a task could involve several unexciting checks, and that skipping one sometimes created extra work for another person.

In 2018, Jordan joined a recreation team and liked rehearsing coordinated moves. She was not always calm in ordinary disagreements, but found it easier to focus when the group shared a specific task and practiced it beforehand.

During 2020, she helped household members keep track of changing school routines. She liked clear instructions and practical assistance, while long online discussions with no next step often left her restless and unsure how to contribute.

At twelve, Jordan became curious about first aid through a community demonstration. In 2023, she asked about the difference between introductory practice and the training required before someone could take responsibility for an actual emergency.

Across 2024 and 2025, she attended an introductory first-aid course and repeated scenarios with an instructor. Immediate trained care and team procedures appealed more than years of diagnostic follow-up, though she had never independently helped in an emergency.

At sixteen in 2026, Jordan is investigating Texas EMT courses and related training. She is willing to examine varied hours rather than assuming she will tolerate them, and values practical service more than expensive travel or an impressive-sounding role.

avoids: Long discussions without a next step
ambitions: Investigate EMT and related introductory training
She imagines a dependable home life, useful work, and ordinary time with people she trusts.
practicalConstraints: Age and entry requirements need checking

biography.selfDescription: I like practicing until a sequence makes sense with the rest of the team. I do not know how I would feel in a real emergency, and I want to understand the hours and responsibilities before I make a bigger decision.
openQuestions: How would real unpredictability affect her?
What work hours and training demands would fit her life?

questions.scene: In a fictional care setting, several observations about a seriously ill person are changing. A trained team must interpret those findings, recognize instability, and decide what care is appropriate within each person’s role.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Using no real symptoms or medical decisions, imagine a timeline with several changing observations. Consider whether you would want to learn how trained people distinguish important changes from uncertain ones.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore learning to interpret clinical changes and choose appropriate immediate care within a defined role? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: This miniature supplies no diagnostic guidance and cannot test readiness to make clinical decisions.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to interpret changing symptoms and clinical findings to recognize instability and choose appropriate immediate care within the clinical responsibilities of your role?

questions.scene: A fictional patient’s measurements and test results form a changing picture. Trained caregivers compare information over time to recognize deterioration and work out the immediate care needed.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine a page of fictional observations labeled earlier, now, and uncertain, with no medical values. Think about whether learning to connect changes across these sources interests you in this clinical setting.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore interpreting changing patient measurements and test results to identify deterioration and immediate care needs? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: This exercise teaches no interpretation of medical values and cannot establish clinical decision-making ability.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to interpret changes in a patient's measurements and test results to recognize deterioration and work out what immediate care is needed?

questions.scene: Continuous care of a critically ill person includes prescribed treatments, checks on the response, and prompt action when dangerous changes occur. Handoffs must keep the next caregiver fully informed.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine handing over a fictional care record organized into prescribed actions, response, and unresolved concerns. Consider whether you would want to learn about maintaining that responsibility through a continuous care shift.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore providing prescribed treatments and coordinating continuous care while responding promptly to dangerous changes? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: A record outline does not reproduce treatment responsibility, sustained vigilance, or the demands of a critical condition.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to provide prescribed treatments and respond promptly to dangerous changes while coordinating continuous nursing care for patients in a critical condition?

biography.name: Sage

background.family: Lives with her mother and an older sibling.
background.finances: Stable modest income; predictable expenses matter.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family regularly helps with community events.
background.school: Public high school with student clubs and general business coursework.
background.accessOpportunities: Club sign-up tools and adult feedback; little difficult-customer experience.

timeline.story: In 2014, Sage enjoyed pretending to run a library for stuffed animals and deciding who would borrow each book. She also liked spontaneous sidewalk games and sometimes forgot the library entirely once the weather improved.

At six, she began leaving short reminder notes for family members. During 2017, one note caused confusion because it omitted the day, and she learned that a message could be neatly written but still fail to tell someone what they needed.

In 2018, Sage helped a teacher prepare a list for a class activity. She liked seeing everyone know where to go next, while a science demonstration and a simple repair project felt interesting only briefly.

During 2020, she used a calendar to manage school calls and helped her household distinguish changed times from canceled plans. She enjoyed clear messages, though repeated last-minute changes sometimes made her take a schedule problem personally.

At twelve, Sage joined a club event team and maintained a sign-up sheet. In 2023, duplicate entries caused confusion, and an adult helped her correct the list without embarrassing the students who had submitted it twice.

Across 2024 and 2025, she continued accurate appointment lists and messages for school activities. An office or service setting sounded more appealing than laboratories or repairs, but she had little experience with customers who were angry, unclear, or unwilling to wait.

At sixteen in 2026, Sage is comparing Texas certificate and degree routes without choosing a final occupation. She wants predictable work and modest spending, while asking how ordinary office responsibilities differ from the small events she already knows.

enjoys: A group knowing what comes next
ambitions: Compare certificates and degrees
She imagines a steady home, modest spending, and enough time for family and familiar social activities.

biography.selfDescription: I like when one clear message saves everyone three confused conversations. Keeping a school list is familiar, but I still need to see how it feels when people need help and are not especially patient about it.
openQuestions: How would difficult service interactions affect her?
Which kinds of office tasks remain interesting through repetition?

questions.scene: A shared record is useful to several teams but contains private information and must be kept for a set period. Access, retention, and eventual secure disposal need rules that fit together.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Using a fictional record only, imagine deciding who needs the full record, who needs a limited version, and what you must learn before setting a deletion date.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore balancing useful access, confidentiality, retention duties, and secure disposal? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: This example does not provide legal retention rules or establish readiness to handle confidential records.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to coordinate document-handling rules that balance useful access with confidentiality, retention duties, and secure disposal when records are no longer needed?

questions.scene: Several departments need reliable help from a small support team. Someone must organize staff responsibilities and the service budget while checking that essential requests are actually completed.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine three requests arriving together: a missing essential supply, a routine record update, and a room booking next month. Consider what you would ask before assigning staff time and funds.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore overseeing support staff and budgets while being accountable for reliable help? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Choosing an order for three requests does not establish interest in ongoing staff supervision and budget responsibility.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to oversee support staff and service budgets while making sure departments receive reliable administrative help?

biography.name: Gabriel Soto

background.family: Lives with his mother and aunt; an older cousin nearby is his usual sounding board.
background.finances: Modest but predictable household income; optional purchases and trips need advance saving.
background.geography: El Paso, Texas, in a neighborhood with several generations of extended family nearby.
background.cultureLanguages: Uses English and Spanish daily, reading more quickly in English; family members often disagree vigorously over dinner.
background.school: Public high school with a small discussion club and a library he uses during lunch.
background.accessOpportunities: Internet is reliable, but there is one shared laptop. His aunt attended college and can explain some procedures, although she is often unavailable during the week.

timeline.story: Gabriel asked adults why signs on the same street used different words for similar things. He liked being read stories with repeated phrases and corrected anyone who skipped one. He was also impatient with puzzles, sometimes pushing pieces together until his aunt persuaded him to look at their shapes.

He liked a classroom game where children decided whether a statement about an animal could be true. He would bring up exceptions long after everyone else moved on. During a school performance he forgot a short line and became determined to avoid the next performance, despite enjoying rehearsals with friends.

A disagreement about a game rule led him to read the entire instruction booklet and mark the relevant sentence. He won that argument but discovered his cousin no longer wanted to play. Around the same time he became enthusiastic about drawing maps, then stopped when he found shading them tedious.

Gabriel read two conflicting explanations of a local water restriction and asked his aunt which details each left out. She encouraged him but grew tired of discussing it every evening. He began writing paragraphs in a notebook, enjoying the chance to revise a sentence before anyone could respond.

In class he wrote a careful response to a disputed school rule and was upset when a teacher said his tone sounded contemptuous. He revised it reluctantly. He tried a speaking competition once, disliked waiting under the lights, and found that remembering his points did not prevent his voice from shaking.

He joined a discussion club that allowed written contributions. He compared competing claims about a community issue, separating the factual disagreements from different priorities. Friends appreciated his explanations but sometimes wanted him to stop correcting minor wording. He also took up casual jogging because it required little conversation or equipment.

Gabriel is writing a longer piece about a contested school policy, checking quotations against original documents when he can find them. He enjoys constructing a reasoned argument and dislikes imagining himself presenting it aloud. He has delayed sharing the draft because one missing fact bothers him, and he knows he may be using that gap as cover.

enjoys: Revising a paragraph until its meaning is precise
avoids: Being asked for an instant opinion
demonstratedSkills: Distinguishing factual disagreement from differing priorities
unfamiliarActivities: Speaking to a large audience regularly
motivations: Avoiding an argument based on a careless claim
ambitions: Publish something classmates choose to read
Become less defensive about feedback
Visit a place he has only read about
struggles: Can sound dismissive when correcting details
Shaky public delivery makes him withdraw
supports: An aunt who discusses sources when free
A cousin who gives blunt feedback
A club sponsor accepting written participation

biography.selfDescription: A claim can sound obvious until you ask what would count as evidence against it. I also know saying that at dinner can be annoying.
openQuestions: Will he share work before every uncertainty is resolved?
How does he respond when a careful argument changes nobody's mind?

questions.scene: A group wants to understand how people experience a shared service. A few vivid stories may miss common experiences, so information needs to be gathered systematically from the group.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine a fictional group asking whether its meeting times work for members. Consider what you would need to learn from more than the two most vocal people.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore systematically gathering information about what a group thinks, experiences, or does? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Being curious about people does not establish interest in systematic survey research.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to investigate what a group of people thinks, experiences, or does by gathering information systematically rather than relying on anecdotes?

questions.scene: An organization suspects that money or property has been misrepresented. A discrepancy could reflect deception, a mistake, or an incomplete record, so the question needs investigation rather than an immediate accusation.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine a fictional item listed as purchased but not found in storage. Identify two explanations besides deliberate wrongdoing that evidence would need to distinguish.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore investigating suspected deception involving money or property by working from evidence? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Enjoying a mystery does not establish interest in careful financial or property investigations.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to investigate suspected deception involving money or property and work out what happened from evidence rather than assumptions?
